latin.2320: THESIS I. AD intelligentiam & elucidationem multarum quaestionum, quae circa gratiam & liberum arbitrium, magna contentione animorum, agitantur, plurimum conducit nosse varias acceptiones & distinctiones gratiae, quae usitatae sunt in Scholis Christianis. Itaque non parum facit ad scopum nostrum, qui est lucem aliquam inferre controversiis illis, quae Scholas Christianas exercent & dividunt, si acceptiones & distinctiones istas, quantum fieri poterit, breviter & dilucide exponamus.
latin.2321: II. Ut autem a Schola Romana ordiamur, observant ejus Theologi, ut inter alios Bellarminus * & Gulielmus Estius, † gratiae vocabulum generalissime sumptum bifariam accipi. Et primo quidem notare ipsum Dei amorem & benevolentiam, per quam hominibus bene vult & facit: deinde etiam quodcunque gratuitum Dei beneficium, & omne illud quod gratiose nobis a Deo conceditur. Ac duplicem hanc gratiae notionem usitatam esse agnoscunt, tum in scriptura divina, tum apud scriptores Ecclesiasticos, & ipsos etiam Scholasticos Doctores. Priorem illam gratiam, gratiam aeternam & increatam vocant: alteram vero gratiam temporariam & creatam. Et eodem recedit quod alii, cum Estio, dicunt, Gratiam, scilicet, intelligi posse, vel ex parte Dei, vel ex parte nostra. * Lib. 1. de gratia & lib. Arb. c. 1. & 2. † In dist. 26. lib. 2. sententiarum Sect. 1.
latin.2322: III. Porro cum non solum quae naturam superant gratuito nobis a Deo donentur, sed ipsa naturae bona, absque ullis nostris meritis, ex gratuita Dei benignitate habeamus, idcirco gratia latissime sumpta, ut Doctores iidem observant, naturae non opponitur, sed naturam ipsam comprehendit: quae quandoque gratiae nomine designatur, propterea quod est gratuitum quoddam Dei beneficium, gratis nobis a Deo collatum. Verum haec acceptio gratiae est quidem frequens in usu communi, in quo naturae dotes atque commoda gratiae divinae ascribere solemus, sed in scripturis & Scholis rarissima, & parum usitata est. Plerunque enim ibi gratia restringitur ad illa Dei beneficia quae naturae ordinem excedunt, neque ex natura fluunt, aut ad eam constituendam & conservandam necessaria sunt, sed ex gratuita Dei benignitate ipsi superaddita.
latin.2323: IV. Et hoc sensu gratia opponitur naturae. Quoniam illa dona quae nobis supra naturam a Deo conferuntur, singulari quodam modo gratuita sunt: quia, scilicet, non tantum sub meritum personae non cadunt, sed neque naturae debentur. Quamvis enim Deus absolute nihil cuiquam debeat, neque ad quicquam obligetur, tamen ex hypothesi quod creaturam velit esse & operari, illi quodammodo ea praestare debet, sine quibus nec esse, nec operari potest.
latin.2324: V. Caeterum gratia illa naturae opposita a nonnullis Scholae Romanae Doctoribus sedulo distinguitur in eam quae homini ante lapsum collata est, & eam quae homini lapso per meritum Christi confertur. Ac priorem illam gratiam vocant, gratiam Adami: Posteriorem vero gratiam Christi. Prior ab illis dicitur gratia sanitatis: haec vero posterior gratia Medicinalis. Prior collata est homini non merenti: posterior etiam indigno.
latin.2325: VI. Hanc distinctionem, ut maximi momenti, saepius inculcat & urget Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis libro cui fecit titulum Augustinus. Ubi gratiae istius utriusque discrimen, prolixe ex Augustino colligit & explicat. Illud autem discrimen in eo constituit, quod gratia data homini ante lapsum adjutorium erat, sine quo primus homo non poterat velle bonum; sed quod non praestabat ut bonum actu vellet. Gratia vero quam Christus homini lapso largitur, efficit ut homo actu velit, & est auxilium, non simpliciter sine quo, sed quo ipsum velle bonum in homine producitur.
latin.2326: VII. Nam observat vir ille adjutoria voluntatis duplicis esse generis. Adjutorium unum esse sine quo voluntas velle non potest, sic tamen ut velle & nolle, uti vel non uti adjutorio, in ejus libero relinquatur arbitrio: aliud quo fit determinate ut voluntas velit. Ac gratiam hominis integri pertendit adjutorium fuisse primi generis, gratiam vero qua Christus hominem corruptum sanat adjutorium secundi generis. In eo, inquit, utriusque gratiae, sanitatis & medicinalis differentia in eo sita est, quod illius primae integritatis adjutorium sic adjuvabat voluntatem, ut cum eo operaretur ipsa, si vellet; nunc autem ipsum adjutorium facit ut velit. Hoc est, adjutorium ante ruinam erat tale, ut influxus adjutorii, perinde atque voluntatis in opus, ab ipso liberae voluntatis nutu penderet, adeoque salva maneret illa libertatis in utramque partem flexibilis indifferentia: nunc vero post ruinam tale est, ut faciat annuere, & influere, & velle voluntatem. De Gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 2. cap. 4.
latin.2327: VIII. Quibus conformiter toto opere docet praecipuum hoc esse discrimen inter gratiam primi Adae & secundi Adae, quod illa dabat operari bonum, si homo vellet: haec dat insuper ut velit. Illa subjecta fuerat nutui & potestativo dominio voluntatis: haec suo nutui & dominio voluntatem subjicit. Illa pedissequali obsequio ductum voluntatis sequebatur: haec imperioso principatu voluntatem trahit quasi pedissequam. Illa superabiliter & declinabiliter voluntatem praeeuntem comitabatur: haec insuperabiliter & indeclinabiliter voluntatem subsequentem ducit & agit.
latin.2328: IX. Verum quanquam hac in parte Jansenius multos sectatores habeat, eos nempe qui singulari modo se discipulos Augustini vocant, haec tamen illius doctrina rejicitur a maxima Scholae Romanae parte: eique palam repugnant, tam qui Molinae Jesuitae Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, quam qui recentiores Thomistae appellantur. Nam priores illi volunt gratiam Christi, non minus quam gratiam primo homini nondum lapso collatam, sic in potestate voluntatis esse, ut pro innata libertate, illa uti, vel non uti possit, & reipsa saepe non utatur: adeoque a libero arbitrio pendere, ut gratia Christi sit efficax, vel non efficax; & effectum suum in hominis conversione obtineat, vel non obtineat.
latin.2329: X. Contra vero qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores, putant gratiam praedeterminantem, & voluntatem ad bonum efficaciter applicantem ab innocentiae statu non fuisse alienam. Et Adam, si quid boni ante peccatum egit, ut egit proculdubio, illud egisse vi cujusdam gratiae Physice voluntatem illius praedeterminantis, eique non tantum boni facultatem largientis, sed illam efficaciter ad bonum praemoventis; sine qua efficaci Dei praemotione, voluntas hominis in nullo ejus statu, juxta ipsorum principia, ad bonum ferri potest.
latin.2330: XI. Porro gratia quae per Christum homini corrupto confertur, communiter in Schola Romana distingui solet, in gratiam quam vocant gratis datam, & in gratiam gratum facientem. Quae partitio, ex Doctorum Scholae istius mente, sic accipienda non est, quasi aliqua sit gratia non gratis data; nam quam vocant gratum facientem agnoscunt etiam esse gratuito donatam: Sed quod alibi saepe fit, uni speciei quae proprio nomine caret, relinquunt nomen generis, ut monet Bellarminus loco supra citato.
latin.2331: XII. Igitur gratia gratis data ipsis est donum supernaturale, absque ullo debito, ad aliorum spiritualem salutem praecipue collatum. Gratia vero gratum faciens donum supernaturale, absque ullo debito, ad propriam uniuscujusque salutem spiritualem potissimum datum. Licet enim commune sit gratiae gratis datae cum gratia gratum faciente, ut tam propriae quam alienae saluti conducant: tamen illud interest, quod gratia gratum faciens datur potissimum ad propriam salutem illius qui accipit; secundario vero ad salutem aliorum: nimirum ut nos ipsi primum sancti justique efficiamur, deinde caeteri videant opera nostra bona, & glorificent Patrem nostrum qui in coelis est. Contra vero gratia gratis data alienam salutem spectat praecipue. Constat enim iis donis quae directe & per se, ad salutem ejus in quo sunt, non conducunt; sed multum juvant ad alios ad poenitentiam & fidem adducendos.
latin.2332: XIII. Itaque ad gratiam gratis datam pertinent sermo scientiae, sermo sapientiae, donum prophetiae, discretio spirituum, genera linguarum, operatio virtutum, gratia sanitatum, & plura ejusmodi quae Apostolus enumerat capite duodecimo prioris ad Corinthios, inter quae dona quaedam sunt, ex quibus beneficia corporalia consequuntur, ut bona valetudo, ex gratia sanitatum; sed quia praecipuus atque ultimus finis omnis gratiae gratis datae est salus animae sempiterna, idcirco omnem ejusmodi gratiam, ad aliorum salutem spiritualem conferri in superius allata definitione dictum est.
latin.2333: XIV. Sub gratia vero gratum faciente comprehendunt ea omnia in quibus aliqua pars, vel initium salutis & justitiae consistit: & quae hominem vel Deo gratum & amicum reddunt, vel ad reconciliationem & amicitiam cum Deo disponunt, & ad hoc per se diriguntur. In quo genere sunt fides, spes, bona voluntas, imo qualecunque fidei, & bonae voluntatis initium, poenitentia, remissio peccatorum, charitas, justitia, bona opera, virtutes earumque augmenta, perseverantia, ac denique vita aeterna, ad quam, tanquam ad gratiam consummatam, priora illa Dei beneficia destinantur. Et de qua dicit Apostolus Rom. 6. Gratia Dei vita aeterna. Ut videre est apud Estium in 2. sentent. dist. 26. paragr. 1.
latin.2334: XV. Porro gratiam illam gratum facientem vocant, quia aliquid in homine ponit quod Deo placet, eique probatur, & hominem, quadantenus saltem, & aliquo respectu, Deo gratum & placentem reddit. Neque tamen eorum mens est, gratiam illam quam in homine ponunt, & gratum facientem vocant, omnem divinae dilectionis actum erga nos praevenire, & esse proprie causam amoris quo Deus hominem prosequitur. Nam docent gratiam illam esse simul divini amoris effectum & objectum. Procedit enim ab illo amore, quo Deus homini bene vult: cum sit maximum bonum quod Deus homini conferat: & eatenus est amore divino posterior. Sed simul est aliquid Deo maxime placens, & cujus respectu homo non potest non esse Deo gratus: & eatenus est objectum divini amoris, & divinam erga nos dilectionem aliqua ratione praecedit.
latin.2335: XVI. Caeterum gratiam gratum facientem Schola Romana dividit in gratiam actualem, & gratiam habitualem, seu quod pene eodem recidit, in gratiam permanentem, & gratiam Auxilii specialis, ut mavult loqui Bellarm. lib. 1. de Gratia & libero Arbitrio cap. 2. Et revera discrimen aliquod notari potest inter gratiam actualem, & inter gratiam istam auxilii specialis. Nam per gratiam quae dicitur auxilii specialis, non ipsae bonae actiones nostrae, sed potius eorum quoddam principium significatur: bona vero nostra opera sunt gratia quaedam actualis, & sub ea comprehenduntur.
latin.2336: XVII. Verum haec divisio, quanquam communiter recepta, a non nemine tamen improbata est. Nam quod sit aliqua Dei Actualis in homine gratia, a nullo quidem inter Theologos Ecclesiae Romanae unquam dubitatum fuit. At vero secus est de gratia habituali. Agnoscunt enim Doctores Scholastici, in Ecclesia Romana rem non fuisse antehac ita certam, & videri solum definitam esse in Concilio Viennensi sub Clemente V. & in Synodo Tridentina superiori saeculo: prius vero fuisse aliquatenus dubium atq; problematicum, An daretur aliqua gratia habitualis.
latin.2337: XVIII. Et certe Albertus Pighius Doctor non incelebris, paulo ante tempora Concilii Tridentini, ausus est hac in parte communi sententiae Scholae Romanae sese opponere. Haec enim, referente Bellarmino, sunt illius verba libro quinto de Libero Arbitrio. Gratiae acceptionem variam, non ex Scholis, sed ex divinis scripturis petemus. Quandoquidem in illis fere imaginantur qualitatem aliquam increatam animae nostrae a Deo; vel eandem cum charitatis habitu, vel distinctam ab eodem. Quae commentitia universa existimo, nec ex scripturis ullam authoritatem habere.
latin.2338: XIX. Et quanquam hodie nullus est post Concilium Tridentinum, qui Pighium sequatur; & sententia ejus communiter damnetur, saltem ut valde temeraria: nihilominus adhuc inter se disputant Scholae Romanae Theologi An de fide sit dari gratiam habitualem, & an Concilia praedicta intenderint rem illam, tanquam de fide definire. Quod post Concilium Tridentinum, negavit Dominicus Soto Doctor insignis, qui illi interfuit. Licet communiter alii sentiant probabilius esse quod dogma istud sit de fide.
latin.2339: XX. Jam autem sub gratia habituali comprehendunt omnes habitus virtutum infusos, ac praesertim gratiam illam in qua consistere volunt justitiam per quam formaliter coram Deo justificamur: quae ab iis dicitur Gratia justificans, & plerumque Gratia simpliciter & sine addito: & ad quam in communi usu, gratiae gratum facientis nomen restringi solet.
latin.2340: XXI. Etenim sciendum est apud scriptores Ecclesiae Romanae, gratiam gratum facientem ordinarie sumi sensu longe strictiore, quam sumitur in modo allata divisione. Juxta quam ita opponitur gratiae gratis datae, ut sub se comprehendat omne donum internum, quod per se salutem accipientis juvat, atque ad eam dirigitur. Nam per gratiam gratum facientem intelligunt habitum & qualitatem quandam, per quam homo proprie & formaliter justus constituitur; adeoque simpliciter Deo gratus & amicus. De qua gratia multas inter se versant quaestiones, quarum haec praecipua est, An gratia illa sit habitus aliquis a charitate distinctus, an vero omnino idem cum charitate.
latin.2341: XXII. Et quidem Thomas Scholae Romanae princeps, & alii plurimi docent gratiam illam justificantem & gratum facientem esse qualitatem quandam realiter distinctam a charitate, & reliquis omnibus habitibus virtutum. Quippe volunt gratiae subjectum esse ipsam animae substantiam, in qua immediate sedem suam habeat: charitatis autem, & aliarum virtutum subjectum esse animae potentias, mentem, scilicet, atque voluntatem. Existimant enim ita se habere gratiam ad virtutes infusas, quemadmodum se habet anima ad suas potentias. Et sicut anima dat esse naturale corpori; ex ipsa autem potentiae fluunt, quae sunt animae instrumenta: sic etiam gratiam, de qua jam quaestio est, dare animae esse quoddam supernaturale: ex ipsa vero quodammodo fluere habitus virtutum infusarum, quae sunt principia proxima operationis supernaturalis.
latin.2342: XXIII. Nonnulli contra, ut Durandus, nihil omnino interesse volunt inter gratiam, & charitatem: ac nequidem ratione, sed solo nomine distingui affirmant. Neque magis distinctas esse charitatem & gratiam, quam esse charum & gratum. Gratiam enim dici, quia per illam homo fit Deo gratus: charitatem vero, quoniam per illam homo redditur Deo charus.
latin.2343: XXIV. Sed alii magno numero mediam quodammodo viam insistunt. Dicunt enim gratiam & charitatem neque omnino esse indistinctas, neque tamen reipsa, sed solum ratione distingui. Nimirum haec est eorum sententia, unum atque eundem habitum, qua parte subjectum respicit, atque hominem ipsum in quo inest exornat, Deoque gratum & amabilem reddit, gratiam nominari: qua parte vero respicit opus, & voluntatem promptam efficit ad Deum super omnia diligendum, illum proprie dici charitatem. Quae sententia est Bellarmini lib. 1. de Gratia & Lib. Arbitrio cap. 6.
latin.2344: XXV. Quod attinet ad gratiam actualem, sive, ut loquitur Bellarminus, gratiam Auxilii specialis, ut quid eo nomine designent intelligatur, notandum est primo auxilia quibus Deus hominem in agendo adjuvat, in Scholis distingui solere in interna, & externa. Externa sunt occasiones & opportunitates agendi, exempla, consilia, praecepta, hortationes, & plura quae singula persequi longum esset: interna in quibusdam animi motibus consistunt. Auxilia externa non pertinent ad gratiam illam de qua jam quaestio est, sed ad interna restringitur.
latin.2345: XXVI. Rursus illud Dei auxilium internum, quo homines in agendo egent, Schola Romana distinguit in Generale & in speciale. Auxilium generale vocant, illud quo Deus cum omnibus creaturis concurrit, & in agendo iis cooperatur, sive bene, sive etiam male agant: sive ea quae faciunt sint intra naturae vires atque modum, sive naturam quadantenus superent. Nam juxta communem Scholae Romanae sensum, in ipsis malis actibus quod positivum est bonum est, nec fieri nisi Deo cooperante potest. Auxilium vero speciale dicitur, quod non datur a Deo, nisi ad actus bonos, & qui vires naturae excedunt. Ac proinde gratia auxilii specialis a Bellarmino definitur, Motio Dei qua homo ad operationes, quae naturam suam aliquo modo superant, adjuvatur.
latin.2346: XXVII. Observat autem ille operationem aliquam tribus modis naturae vires superare posse. Primo simpliciter & absolute. Ut si operatio ex suo genere sit ordinis altioris quam sint res naturales. Quales sunt actus virtutum Theologicarum fidei, spei, & charitatis, quae non acquiruntur per iteratos & frequentatos actus, sed divinitus in animam infunduntur. Secundo non simpliciter, sed ratione status peccati; quoniam homo per peccatum debilitatus multa non potest sine tali auxilio facile efficere. Tertio ratione modi, loci, temporis, aut alterius cujuslibet circumstantiae: quoniam contingere potest, ut id quod neque ex genere suo, neque ratione status, vires naturae superat, easdem tamen superet ratione circumstantiae. Ita, inquit, poterit homo justus praeceptum aliquod Decalogi facile adimplere, si nulla extrinsecus diabolica tentatio accedat. Si vero ejusmodi tentatio accedat, sine speciali auxilio id facere non poterit.
latin.2347: XXVIII. Itaque ad gratiam actualem pertinent, ex doctorum Scholae Romanae sententia, omnes boni & salutares motus, quos in animis nostris Deus excitat. Qui motus & Dei sunt, quoniam ab eo procedunt: & nostri quoque, quoniam sunt actiones vitales, a facultatibus nostris, Deo speciali modo movente, elicitae.
latin.2348: XXIX. Boni autem illi motus, vel intellectum spectant, quales sunt internae illuminationes & cogitationes piae a Deo immissae, ac uno verbo quaelibet illustrationes & inspirationes, quibus mens in veritatis salutiferae notitiam ducitur: vel voluntatem, ut pia desideria & salutares motus atque affectus, quibus immediate voluntas afficitur.
latin.2349: XXX. Rursus autem Gregorius de Valentia, clarioris doctrinae causa, motus qui ad actualem gratiam reducuntur, in duo genera distinguit. Unum, inquit, continetur iis motibus, quibus Deus mentes nostras excitat, vocat, & invitat, ut ad ipsum per fidem, spem, charitatem, poenitentiam, & hujusmodi actiones convertantur. Alterum continetur his motibus, seu actionibus, quibus Deo excitanti, vocanti, & invitanti respondemus, & aperimus mentis nostrae januam, quum ad eum convertimur. Tomo 2. Disput. 8. quaestione 3. puncto 2.
latin.2350: XXXI. Prioris generis motus, juxta ipsum, sunt indeliberati, & physice tantum non libere a facultatibus nostris eliciti: posterioris vero liberi sunt & deliberati. Ad prius genus pertinent piae cogitationes & pia desideria, absque nostro consensu immediate a Deo immissa: ad posterius vero, omnes virtutum Christianarum actus, quos Dei gratia juvante elicimus.
latin.2351: XXXII. Praeterea gratia auxilii specialis, sive, ut aliis dicitur, actualis, dividi solet in gratiam excitantem, & gratiam adjuvantem; seu, ut loquitur Bellarminus, in auxilium excitans, & auxilium adjuvans. Quae distinctio non eodem modo a Theologis Scholae Romanae exponitur. Bellarminus, & omnes cum eo Jesuitae, aliique plurimi, ad gratiam excitantem, quam vocantem etiam appellant, dicunt pertinere divinas illustrationes, & inspirationes, quibus Deus cor nostrum pulsat, ut a somno peccati, vel negligentiae in bonis operibus excitemur. Ad gratiam autem adjuvantem, seu auxilii adjuvantis, spectare divinam cooperationem, directionem, & protectionem, quibus juvamur, tum ut eligamus, tum ut faciamus quod Deus praeveniens inspiravit. Juxta illud Apoc. 3. Ecce sto ad ostium & pulso, si quis audierit vocem meam, intrabo ad illum, &c. Quae sunt verba Bellarmini lib. 1. de lib. Arbitrio cap. 2.
latin.2352: XXXIII. Atque eodem recidit expositio Gregorii de Valentia. Nam gratiam vocantem, seu excitantem, inquit, appellant Theologi divinas quasdam inspirationes, seu motus quosdam divinitus in mente hominis excitatos, quibus Deus hominem ad se allicit & invitat, & ad actiones pias atque salutares movet, ut fidei, spei, charitatis, & poenitentiae actibus convertatur. Gratiam autem adjuvantem appellant, Dei dona & beneficia, quibus Deus hominem divinae vocationi & excitationi consentientem adjuvat, tum in eo ipso quod consentit & convertitur, tum in aliis actionibus pietatis, per quas contenditur ad beatitudinem. Itaq; ad hanc gratiam adjuvantem in primis pertinet quod Deus peculiari concursu cum homine cooperatur ad conversionem, id est, ad credendum, sperandum, diligendum, poenitendum, &c. Item quod hominem singulari cura & providentia custodit, & protegit a malo, & dirigit atque stimulat ab bonum, & ei variis inspirationibus, ad vincendas tentationes, & ad observanda mandata robur praebet. Tom. 2. disput. 8. quaest. 3. punct. 3.

sections.title: Why the distinctions of grace must be set out
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. For the understanding and elucidation of many questions, which concerning grace and free choice, with great contention of minds, are agitated, it conduces very much to know the various acceptations and distinctions of grace, which are in use in the Christian Schools. And so it does not do little for our aim, which is to bring some light to those controversies, which exercise and divide the Christian Schools, if we set out those acceptations and distinctions, as far as can be done, briefly and clearly.
pass_b: Thesis I. Many questions about grace and free choice are argued with great heat, and to understand and clear them up it helps a great deal to know the various senses and distinctions of grace used in the Christian schools.
Our aim is to throw some light on the controversies that occupy and divide those schools. So it will serve that aim well if we set out these senses and distinctions as briefly and clearly as we can.

sections.title: Grace taken most generally: God's love, and any free gift
sections.pass_a: II. But that we may begin from the Roman School, its Theologians observe, as among others Bellarmine and William Estius, that the word grace taken most generally is accepted in two ways. And first indeed to denote the very love and benevolence of God, by which he wills well and does well to men: then also whatever gratuitous benefit of God, and all that which is graciously granted to us by God. And they acknowledge that this twofold notion of grace is in use, both in divine scripture, and among Ecclesiastical writers, and even the Scholastic Doctors themselves. That former grace they call eternal and uncreated grace: but the other temporary and created grace. And to the same comes back what others, with Estius, say, that grace, namely, can be understood, either on the part of God, or on our part.
pass_b: Thesis II. To begin with the Roman School: its theologians, Bellarmine and William Estius among others, observe that the word 'grace', taken in its most general sense, is used in two ways.

First it means God's own love and goodwill, by which he wishes men well and does them good. Second, it means any free benefit from God, anything he grants us graciously. They acknowledge that both senses are current in Holy Scripture, in the church writers, and in the scholastic doctors themselves.
The first they call eternal and uncreated grace, the second temporal and created grace. What others say with Estius comes to the same thing: grace can be understood either on God's side or on ours.

sections.title: Grace taken most widely includes nature itself
sections.pass_a: III. Further since not only the things which surpass nature are given to us gratuitously by God, but the goods of nature themselves, without any merits of ours, we have from the gratuitous kindness of God, therefore grace taken most widely, as the same Doctors observe, is not opposed to nature, but comprehends nature itself: which sometimes is designated by the name of grace, because it is a certain gratuitous benefit of God, freely conferred on us by God. But this acceptation of grace is indeed frequent in common use, in which we are accustomed to ascribe the endowments and advantages of nature to divine grace, but in the scriptures and Schools most rare, and little used. For mostly there grace is restricted to those benefits of God which exceed the order of nature, and neither flow from nature, nor are necessary for constituting and conserving it, but by the gratuitous kindness of God are added over to it.
pass_b: Thesis III. God gives us freely not only what surpasses nature: the goods of nature themselves we also have from his free kindness, without any merit of ours. So grace in its widest sense, as the same doctors observe, is not set against nature but includes nature itself, which is sometimes called grace because it is a free benefit God has given us for nothing.
This sense is common enough in ordinary speech, where we credit the gifts and advantages of nature to God's grace. In Scripture and in the schools it is very rare and little used.

There grace is usually confined to those benefits of God that go beyond the order of nature: they do not flow from nature and are not needed to make it what it is or to preserve it, but are added to it by God's free kindness.

lemmas.latin: gratia latissime sumpta, ut Doctores iidem observant, naturae non opponitur
lemmas.gloss: grace taken most widely, as the same Doctors observe, is not opposed to nature

lemmas.latin: in quo naturae dotes atque commoda gratiae divinae ascribere solemus

choices.why: The widest sense, under which nature itself counts as grace; Le Blanc notes it is rare in Scripture and the schools.

sections.title: Grace opposed to nature: owed neither to merit nor to nature
sections.pass_a: IV. And in this sense grace is opposed to nature. Because those gifts which are conferred on us by God above nature, are gratuitous in a certain singular manner: because, namely, not only do they not fall under the merit of the person, but neither are they owed to nature. For although God absolutely owes nothing to anyone, nor is obliged to anything, yet on the hypothesis that he wills a creature to be and to operate, he must in a manner furnish to it those things, without which it can neither be, nor operate.
pass_b: Thesis IV. In this sense grace is set against nature. The gifts God confers on us above nature are free in a special way: they do not fall under the person's merit, and they are not owed to nature either.

God, absolutely speaking, owes nothing to anyone and is bound to nothing. Yet once he wills that a creature should exist and act, he must in a way supply it with whatever it cannot exist or act without.

lemmas.latin: singulari quodam modo gratuita sunt
lemmas.gloss: are gratuitous in a certain singular manner

lemmas.latin: non tantum sub meritum personae non cadunt, sed neque naturae debentur
lemmas.gloss: not only do they not fall under the merit of the person, but neither are they owed to nature

lemmas.latin: ex hypothesi quod creaturam velit esse & operari
lemmas.gloss: on the hypothesis that he wills a creature to be and to operate

choices.why: A conditional debt: God owes nothing absolutely, but given his will to create he owes a creature what it needs to be and act.

sections.title: Adam's grace and Christ's grace
sections.pass_a: V. But that grace opposed to nature is by some Doctors of the Roman School carefully distinguished into that which was conferred on man before the fall, and that which is conferred on man fallen through the merit of Christ. And that former grace they call the grace of Adam: but the latter the grace of Christ. The former is called by them the grace of health: but this latter the Medicinal grace. The former was conferred on man not meriting: the latter even on one unworthy.
pass_b: Thesis V. Some doctors of the Roman School take care to divide this grace that is set against nature into two: the grace given to man before the fall, and the grace given to fallen man through Christ's merit.

They call the first the grace of Adam and the second the grace of Christ; the first the grace of health and the second healing grace. The first was given to a man who had not earned it, the second to one who was actually unworthy of it.

lemmas.latin: sedulo distinguitur in eam quae homini ante lapsum collata est
lemmas.gloss: is carefully distinguished into that which was conferred on man before the fall

lemmas.latin: Prior ab illis dicitur gratia sanitatis
lemmas.gloss: The former is called by them the grace of health

lemmas.latin: Prior collata est homini non merenti: posterior etiam indigno
lemmas.gloss: The former was conferred on man not meriting: the latter even on one unworthy

choices.english: the grace of health ... healing grace
choices.why: Jansenius' pair: Adam's grace in the state of health against Christ's medicinal grace for fallen man.

sections.title: Jansenius: Adam's help 'without which', Christ's help 'by which'
sections.pass_a: VI. This distinction, as of the greatest moment, Jansenius Bishop of Ypres more often inculcates and urges in the book to which he gave the title Augustinus. Where the difference of that twofold grace, he copiously gathers and explains out of Augustine. But that difference he places in this, that grace given to man before the fall was a help, without which the first man could not will good; but which did not bring it about that he actually willed good. But the grace which Christ bestows on fallen man, effects that man actually wills, and is a help, not simply without which, but by which the very willing of good is produced in man.
pass_b: Thesis VI. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, presses this distinction again and again as of the greatest weight in the book he titled Augustinus, where he collects and explains the difference between the two graces at length from Augustine.
He puts the difference here. The grace given to man before the fall was a help without which the first man could not will good, but it did not make him actually will it.
The grace Christ gives fallen man makes him actually will. It is not merely a help without which, but a help by which the willing of good is itself produced in him.

lemmas.latin: ut maximi momenti, saepius inculcat & urget
lemmas.gloss: as of the greatest moment, more often inculcates and urges

lemmas.latin: sine quo primus homo non poterat velle bonum; sed quod non praestabat ut bonum actu vellet
lemmas.gloss: without which the first man could not will good; but which did not bring it about that he actually willed good

lemmas.latin: non simpliciter sine quo, sed quo ipsum velle bonum in homine producitur
lemmas.gloss: not simply without which, but by which the very willing of good is produced in man

choices.english: a help without which ... a help by which
choices.why: Augustine's distinction (De correptione et gratia 11-12) as Jansenius uses it: a help needed for willing, against a help that brings about the willing itself.

notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris.
The 'help without which' and 'help by which' (adjutorium sine quo non, adjutorium quo) come from Augustine, De correptione et gratia 11.31-12.34.

sections.title: Jansenius on the two kinds of help (De gratia Christi 2.4)
sections.pass_a: VII. For that man observes that the helps of the will are of a twofold kind. One help to be that without which the will cannot will, yet so that to will and not will, to use or not use the help, is left in its free choice: the other by which it comes about determinately that the will wills. And he contends that the grace of man unfallen was a help of the first kind, but the grace by which Christ heals corrupted man a help of the second kind. In this, he says, the difference of each grace, of health and medicinal, in this is placed, that the help of that first integrity so helped the will, that with it the will itself might work, if it willed; but now the help itself makes that it wills. That is, the help before the ruin was such, that the influx of the help, just as of the will into the work, depended on the very nod of the free will, and so that indifference of liberty flexible to either side remained safe: but now after the ruin it is such, that it makes the will to assent, and to flow in, and to will. Of the Grace of Christ the saviour book 2 chapter 4.
pass_b: Thesis VII. For he observes that the will's helps are of two kinds. One is a help without which the will cannot will, yet in such a way that willing or not willing, using the help or not using it, is left to its free choice. The other is a help by which it is determinately brought about that the will wills.

He holds that the grace of man in his integrity was a help of the first kind, and that the grace by which Christ heals corrupt man is a help of the second kind. 'The difference between the two graces, of health and of healing,' he says, 'lies in this: the help of that first integrity so helped the will that the will itself might work with it, if it chose; now the help itself makes it will.

That is, before the ruin the help was such that its influence on the work, just like the will's, hung on the free will's own nod, so that the indifference of liberty, able to bend either way, remained intact. Now, after the ruin, it is such that it makes the will assent, and flow into the work, and will' (De gratia Christi salvatoris, book 2, chapter 4).

lemmas.gloss: One help to be that without which the will cannot will

lemmas.latin: aliud quo fit determinate ut voluntas velit
lemmas.gloss: the other by which it comes about determinately that the will wills

lemmas.latin: nunc autem ipsum adjutorium facit ut velit
lemmas.gloss: but now the help itself makes that it wills

lemmas.latin: ab ipso liberae voluntatis nutu penderet
lemmas.gloss: depended on the very nod of the free will

lemmas.latin: ut faciat annuere, & influere, & velle voluntatem
lemmas.gloss: that it makes the will to assent, and to flow in, and to will

choices.english: a help without which ... a help by which
choices.why: Augustine's distinction (De correptione et gratia 11-12) as Jansenius uses it: a help needed for willing, against a help that brings about the willing itself.

notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris. The print repeats 'in eo' ('In eo ... differentia in eo sita est'); the lock keeps it and the English renders it once.
'Influere' is rendered 'flow into the work', matching 'influxus ... in opus' earlier in the quotation; 'annuere' is 'assent' (literally 'nod assent').

sections.title: Jansenius' contrasts between the grace of the first and second Adam
sections.pass_a: VIII. In conformity with which through the whole work he teaches this to be the chief difference between the grace of the first Adam and of the second Adam, that that gave to work good, if man willed: this gives besides that he wills. That had been subject to the nod and potestative dominion of the will: this subjects the will to its nod and dominion. That followed the leading of the will with a footman's obedience: this by imperious rule draws the will as if a footman. That accompanied the will going before, surmountably and declinably: this insurmountably and indeclinably leads and drives the will following.
pass_b: Thesis VIII. In keeping with this he teaches throughout the work that the chief difference between the grace of the first Adam and that of the second is this: the first gave man the power to do good if he willed, while the second gives him besides the willing itself.

The first was subject to the will's nod and to its power of command; the second subjects the will to its own nod and command. The first followed the will's lead with the obedience of a servant at its heels; the second, ruling with authority, draws the will after it like such a servant.
The first went along with the will as the will went ahead, and could be overcome and turned aside. The second leads and drives the will as it follows, and can be neither overcome nor turned aside.

lemmas.latin: quod illa dabat operari bonum, si homo vellet: haec dat insuper ut velit
lemmas.gloss: that that gave to work good, if man willed: this gives besides that he wills

lemmas.latin: Illa pedissequali obsequio ductum voluntatis sequebatur
lemmas.gloss: That followed the leading of the will with a footman's obedience

lemmas.latin: haec insuperabiliter & indeclinabiliter voluntatem subsequentem ducit & agit
lemmas.gloss: this insurmountably and indeclinably leads and drives the will following

choices.english: can be neither overcome nor turned aside
choices.why: Jansenius' adverbs for Christ's grace, echoing Augustine's 'indeclinabiliter et insuperabiliter' (De correptione et gratia 12.38).

notes: Cornelius Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, Augustinus (1640), De gratia Christi salvatoris.

sections.title: Molinists against Jansenius: grace in the will's power
sections.pass_a: IX. But although in this part Jansenius has many followers, those namely who in a singular manner call themselves disciples of Augustine, yet this doctrine of his is rejected by the greatest part of the Roman School: and to it openly are opposed, both those who follow the Method and doctrine of Molina the Jesuit, and those who are called the more recent Thomists. For those former will that the grace of Christ, not less than the grace conferred on the first man not yet fallen, is so in the power of the will, that according to innate liberty, it can use it, or not use it, and in fact often does not use it: and so depends on free choice, that the grace of Christ is efficacious, or not efficacious; and obtains its effect in the conversion of man, or does not obtain it.
pass_b: Thesis IX. On this point Jansenius has many followers, namely those who call themselves disciples of Augustine in a special sense. Even so, this teaching of his is rejected by most of the Roman School. Both the followers of the method and teaching of Molina the Jesuit and those called the recent Thomists openly oppose it.

The first group hold that the grace of Christ, no less than the grace given to the first man before he fell, is in the will's power in such a way that, by its inborn liberty, the will can use it or not use it, and in fact often does not.
So, on their view, it depends on free choice whether Christ's grace is efficacious or not, and whether it achieves its effect in a man's conversion or fails to.

lemmas.gloss: who in a singular manner call themselves disciples of Augustine

lemmas.latin: haec tamen illius doctrina rejicitur a maxima Scholae Romanae parte
lemmas.gloss: yet this doctrine of his is rejected by the greatest part of the Roman School

lemmas.latin: ut pro innata libertate, illa uti, vel non uti possit, & reipsa saepe non utatur
lemmas.gloss: that according to innate liberty, it can use it, or not use it, and in fact often does not use it

lemmas.gloss: that the grace of Christ is efficacious, or not efficacious

choices.why: The Dominican school after Báñez, defenders of physical premotion; 'recent' sets them off from Thomas himself.

notes: Luis de Molina SJ, Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (1588).

sections.title: The recent Thomists: physical predetermination even in Adam
sections.pass_a: X. On the other hand those who are called the more recent Thomists, think that grace predetermining, and efficaciously applying the will to good was not alien from the state of innocence. And that Adam, if he did anything good before sin, as he did without doubt, did it by force of a certain grace Physically predetermining his will, and to it not only bestowing the faculty of good, but efficaciously premoving it to good; without which efficacious premotion of God, the will of man in no state of it, according to their own principles, can be borne to good.
pass_b: Thesis X. Those called the recent Thomists, on the other hand, think that a grace which predetermines the will and applies it efficaciously to good was not foreign to the state of innocence.

If Adam did any good before he sinned, as he certainly did, he did it, they say, by the power of a grace that physically predetermined his will: a grace that did not merely give his will the ability to do good but efficaciously moved it to good beforehand.
On their principles, without this efficacious premotion from God man's will cannot be carried toward good in any of its states.

lemmas.latin: putant gratiam praedeterminantem, & voluntatem ad bonum efficaciter applicantem ab innocentiae statu non fuisse alienam
lemmas.gloss: think that grace predetermining, and efficaciously applying the will to good was not alien from the state of innocence

lemmas.latin: si quid boni ante peccatum egit, ut egit proculdubio
lemmas.gloss: if he did anything good before sin, as he did without doubt

choices.why: The Thomist term for God's prior physical motion of the will to its act; kept as the technical word.

sections.title: Grace freely given and grace that makes pleasing
sections.pass_a: XI. Further the grace which through Christ is conferred on corrupted man, is commonly in the Roman School wont to be distinguished, into the grace which they call freely given, and into the grace making pleasing. Which partition, from the mind of the Doctors of that School, is not to be so taken, as though there were some grace not freely given; for that which they call making pleasing they acknowledge also to be gratuitously given: But as elsewhere often happens, to one species which lacks its proper name, they leave the name of the genus, as Bellarmine warns in the place above cited.
pass_b: Thesis XI. The grace conferred on corrupt man through Christ is commonly divided in the Roman School into what they call grace freely given and the grace that makes pleasing.
In the minds of that School's doctors the division is not meant to imply that some grace is not freely given, for they grant that the grace that makes pleasing is also given freely.
Rather, as often happens elsewhere, one species that has no name of its own is left with the name of the genus, as Bellarmine points out in the place cited above.

lemmas.latin: in gratiam quam vocant gratis datam, & in gratiam gratum facientem
lemmas.gloss: into the grace which they call freely given, and into the grace making pleasing

lemmas.latin: quasi aliqua sit gratia non gratis data
lemmas.gloss: as though there were some grace not freely given

lemmas.latin: uni speciei quae proprio nomine caret, relinquunt nomen generis
lemmas.gloss: to one species which lacks its proper name, they leave the name of the genus

choices.why: Scholastic term for gifts such as prophecy or tongues, given chiefly for others' salvation; Le Blanc notes every grace is free, the name being left to one species.

notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1. (chapters 1-2, cited in Thesis II).

sections.title: The two defined: for others' salvation, or chiefly one's own
sections.pass_a: XII. Therefore grace freely given is to them a supernatural gift, without any debt, conferred chiefly for the spiritual salvation of others. But grace making pleasing a supernatural gift, without any debt, given chiefly for the proper spiritual salvation of each one. For although it is common to grace freely given with grace making pleasing, that they conduce as well to one's own as to another's salvation: yet this differs, that grace making pleasing is given chiefly for the proper salvation of him who receives it; but secondarily for the salvation of others: namely that we ourselves first are made holy and just, then the others may see our good works, and glorify our Father who is in heaven. But on the contrary grace freely given regards chiefly another's salvation. For it consists of those gifts which directly and of themselves, do not conduce to the salvation of him in whom they are; but help much to bring others to repentance and faith.
pass_b: Thesis XII. So for them grace freely given is a supernatural gift, given without any debt, chiefly for the spiritual salvation of others. The grace that makes pleasing is a supernatural gift, given without any debt, chiefly for each person's own spiritual salvation.

Both kinds serve the salvation of the receiver and of others alike. The difference is that the grace that makes pleasing is given chiefly for the salvation of the one who receives it and only secondarily for others: first we ourselves are to be made holy and righteous, and then others are to see our good works and glorify our Father in heaven.

Grace freely given, by contrast, looks chiefly to the salvation of others. It consists of gifts that do not of themselves directly serve the salvation of the person in whom they are, but are a great help in bringing others to repentance and faith.

sections.title: What belongs to grace freely given (1 Corinthians 12)
sections.pass_a: XIII. And so to grace freely given pertain the word of knowledge, the word of wisdom, the gift of prophecy, discerning of spirits, kinds of tongues, working of powers, grace of healings, and more of this kind which the Apostle enumerates in the twelfth chapter of the first to the Corinthians, among which gifts certain ones are, from which bodily benefits follow, as good health, from the grace of healings; but because the chief and last end of all grace freely given is the everlasting salvation of the soul, therefore in the definition brought above it was said that all grace of this kind, is conferred for the spiritual salvation of others.
pass_b: Thesis XIII. Grace freely given therefore includes the word of knowledge, the word of wisdom, the gift of prophecy, the discerning of spirits, kinds of tongues, the working of miracles, the gift of healing, and the other gifts of this kind that the Apostle lists in 1 Corinthians 12.

Some of these gifts bring bodily benefits, as the gift of healing brings good health. But since the chief and final end of all grace freely given is the eternal salvation of the soul, the definition given above said that all such grace is conferred for the spiritual salvation of others.

sections.title: What the grace that makes pleasing includes, up to eternal life
sections.pass_a: XIV. But under grace making pleasing they comprehend all those things in which some part, or beginning of salvation and righteousness consists: and which either render man pleasing and a friend to God, or dispose to reconciliation and friendship with God, and are of themselves directed to this. In which kind are faith, hope, good will, nay any beginning whatever of faith, and of good will, repentance, remission of sins, charity, righteousness, good works, virtues and their increases, perseverance, and finally eternal life, to which, as to grace consummated, those former benefits of God are destined. And of which the Apostle says Rom. 6. The grace of God eternal life. As may be seen in Estius on the 2nd of the Sentences dist. 26. paragr. 1.
pass_b: Thesis XIV. Under the grace that makes pleasing they include everything in which any part or beginning of salvation and righteousness consists: everything that either makes a man pleasing to God and his friend, or disposes him to reconciliation and friendship with God and is of itself directed to that end.

To this class belong faith, hope and good will, indeed any beginning at all of faith and good will; repentance, the forgiveness of sins, charity, righteousness, good works, the virtues and their growth, perseverance, and finally eternal life itself. Those earlier benefits of God are destined for eternal life as for grace brought to completion, and of it the Apostle says, 'The grace of God is eternal life' (Romans 6). So Estius on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 26, paragraph 1.

sections.title: Why 'makes pleasing': both effect and object of God's love
sections.pass_a: XV. Further they call that grace making pleasing, because it puts something in man which pleases God, and is approved by him, and renders man, at least to some extent, and in some respect, pleasing and acceptable to God. Nor yet is it their mind, that that grace which they put in man, and call making pleasing, goes before every act of divine love toward us, and is properly the cause of the love with which God pursues man. For they teach that grace to be at once the effect and object of divine love. For it proceeds from that love, by which God wills well to man: since it is the greatest good which God confers on man: and so far it is posterior to divine love. But at the same time it is something greatly pleasing to God, and in respect of which man cannot not be pleasing to God: and so far it is the object of divine love, and in some way precedes divine love toward us.
pass_b: Thesis XV. They call it the grace that makes pleasing because it places in a man something that pleases God and wins his approval, and so makes the man, at least to some degree and in some respect, pleasing and acceptable to God.

They do not mean that the grace they place in man under that name comes before every act of God's love toward us, or is strictly the cause of the love God bears him. They teach that this grace is at once the effect and the object of God's love.

It comes from the love by which God wishes man well, being the greatest good God bestows on him, and to that extent it comes after God's love. At the same time it is something highly pleasing to God, and because of it a man cannot fail to be pleasing to him. To that extent it is the object of God's love and in some way comes before his love for us.

sections.title: Actual and habitual grace; Bellarmine's 'grace of special help'
sections.pass_a: XVI. But the grace making pleasing the Roman School divides into actual grace, and habitual grace, or what comes almost to the same, into permanent grace, and the grace of special Help, as Bellarm. prefers to speak book 1 of Grace and free Choice chap. 2. And in truth some difference can be noted between actual grace, and that grace of special help. For by the grace which is called of special help, not our good actions themselves, but rather a certain principle of them is signified: but our good works are a certain actual grace, and are comprehended under it.
pass_b: Thesis XVI. The Roman School divides the grace that makes pleasing into actual and habitual grace, or, which comes to nearly the same thing, into permanent grace and the grace of special help, as Bellarmine prefers to put it (De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 2).

There is in fact some difference to be noted between actual grace and this grace of special help. The grace of special help means not our good actions themselves but rather a kind of principle of them, whereas our good works are themselves a kind of actual grace and fall under that term.

sections.title: Habitual grace once doubtful: Vienne and Trent
sections.pass_a: XVII. But this division, although commonly received, has yet been disapproved by someone. For that there is some Actual grace of God in man, was never doubted indeed by anyone among the Theologians of the Roman Church. But it is otherwise of habitual grace. For the Scholastic Doctors acknowledge, that in the Roman Church the thing was not formerly so certain, and seems to have been defined only in the Council of Vienne under Clement V. and in the Synod of Trent in the former century: but before it was to some extent doubtful and problematic, Whether there was given some habitual grace.
pass_b: Thesis XVII. Commonly accepted as this division is, someone has nevertheless rejected it. No theologian of the Roman Church has ever doubted that there is some actual grace of God in man. Habitual grace is another matter.

The scholastic doctors admit that in the Roman Church the point was not formerly so settled. It seems to have been defined only at the Council of Vienne under Clement V and at the Council of Trent in the last century; before that it was somewhat doubtful and open to dispute whether any habitual grace is given.

lemmas.gloss: has yet been disapproved by someone

notes: Council of Vienne (1311-1312) under Clement V, constitution Fidei catholicae, preferring the opinion that infused grace and virtues are given to infants in baptism.
Council of Trent, session 6 (1547), on justification; 'the former century' is the sixteenth, Le Blanc writing in the seventeenth.

sections.title: Pighius against habitual grace
sections.pass_a: XVIII. And certainly Albert Pighius a Doctor not uncelebrated, a little before the times of the Council of Trent, dared in this part to oppose himself to the common opinion of the Roman School. For these, as Bellarmine reports, are his words in the fifth book on Free Choice. The various acceptation of grace, not from the Schools, but from the divine scriptures we will seek. Since in those they mostly imagine some quality created into our soul by God; either the same with the habit of charity, or distinct from it. All which I judge fictitious, and to have no authority from the scriptures.
pass_b: Thesis XVIII. Indeed Albert Pighius, a doctor of some fame, dared on this point to set himself against the common view of the Roman School a little before the time of the Council of Trent.

As Bellarmine reports, these are his words in the fifth book of his work On Free Choice: 'We shall look for the various senses of grace not in the schools but in Holy Scripture. For in the schools they generally imagine some quality created in (increatam) our soul by God, either the same as the habit of charity or distinct from it. I judge all this to be invented, with no authority from Scripture.'

lemmas.latin: Quae commentitia universa existimo
lemmas.gloss: All which I judge fictitious

notes: Albert Pighius, De libero hominis arbitrio et divina gratia (1542), book 5, as reported by Bellarmine.
'Increatam' is read as the participle of increo, 'created in' (the quality God creates in the soul), not 'uncreated'; the dative 'animae nostrae' and 'a Deo' require it.
'In illis' ('in those') refers back to the schools; the English makes this explicit.

sections.title: After Trent: is habitual grace of faith? Soto denies
sections.pass_a: XIX. And although today there is no one after the Council of Trent, who follows Pighius; and his opinion is commonly condemned, at least as very rash: nevertheless still the Theologians of the Roman School dispute among themselves Whether it is of faith that habitual grace is given, and whether the said Councils intended to define that thing, as of faith. Which after the Council of Trent, Dominic Soto a notable Doctor, who was present at it, denied. Although commonly others think it more probable that this dogma is of faith.
pass_b: Thesis XIX. Since the Council of Trent nobody follows Pighius, and his view is commonly condemned, at the least as very rash. Even so, the theologians of the Roman School still argue among themselves whether it is a matter of faith that habitual grace is given, and whether those councils meant to define the point as of faith.
After the Council of Trent, Domingo de Soto, a distinguished doctor who had been present at it, denied that they did. Others commonly hold it more probable that this teaching is of faith.

lemmas.gloss: at least as very rash

lemmas.gloss: Dominic Soto a notable Doctor, who was present at it, denied

choices.why: A doctrine defined so that denying it is heresy; Soto denied Trent had raised habitual grace to that level.

notes: Domingo de Soto OP (1494-1560), theologian at Trent, author of De natura et gratia (1547).

sections.title: Habitual grace includes infused virtues and justifying grace
sections.pass_a: XX. Now under habitual grace they comprehend all the infused habits of virtues, and especially that grace in which they will to consist the righteousness by which formally we are justified before God: which by them is called justifying Grace, and mostly Grace simply and without addition: and to which in common use, the name of grace making pleasing is wont to be restricted.
pass_b: Thesis XX. Under habitual grace they include all the infused habits of the virtues, and above all the grace in which, on their view, consists the righteousness by which we are formally justified before God.
They call this justifying grace, and usually just 'grace' with nothing added, and in common usage the name 'grace that makes pleasing' is usually confined to it.

lemmas.latin: omnes habitus virtutum infusos
lemmas.gloss: all the infused habits of virtues

lemmas.gloss: the righteousness by which formally we are justified before God

lemmas.gloss: Grace simply and without addition

choices.why: Scholastic: the righteousness that is the form of the justified man, inherent rather than imputed; this is the point Protestants contest.

sections.title: The stricter sense of 'grace that makes pleasing'; is it charity?
sections.pass_a: XXI. For it is to be known that among the writers of the Roman Church, grace making pleasing is ordinarily taken in a sense far stricter, than it is taken in the division just brought. According to which it is so opposed to grace freely given, that it comprehends under itself every internal gift, which of itself helps the salvation of the receiver, and is directed to it. For by grace making pleasing they understand a habit and certain quality, by which man is properly and formally constituted righteous; and so simply pleasing and a friend to God. Concerning which grace they turn over many questions among themselves, of which this is the chief, Whether that grace is some habit distinct from charity, or rather altogether the same with charity.
pass_b: Thesis XXI. It should be understood that writers of the Roman Church ordinarily take the grace that makes pleasing in a far narrower sense than in the division just given. There it is set against grace freely given in such a way that it covers every inward gift that of itself helps the receiver's salvation and is directed to it.
In the narrower sense they mean by it a habit, a kind of quality, by which a man is properly and formally made righteous and so simply pleasing to God and his friend.
They debate many questions among themselves about this grace. The chief is whether it is a habit distinct from charity or entirely the same as charity.

lemmas.latin: ordinarie sumi sensu longe strictiore, quam sumitur in modo allata divisione
lemmas.gloss: is ordinarily taken in a sense far stricter, than it is taken in the division just brought

lemmas.latin: per quam homo proprie & formaliter justus constituitur
lemmas.gloss: by which man is properly and formally constituted righteous

lemmas.latin: An gratia illa sit habitus aliquis a charitate distinctus, an vero omnino idem cum charitate
lemmas.gloss: Whether that grace is some habit distinct from charity, or rather altogether the same with charity

choices.why: Scholastic term (Latin gratum faciens) for grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God; kept literal so the contrast with gratia gratis data stays visible.

sections.title: Thomas: grace really distinct from charity, seated in the soul's essence
sections.pass_a: XXII. And indeed Thomas prince of the Roman School, and very many others teach that justifying grace and making pleasing to be a certain quality really distinct from charity, and from all the other habits of virtues. Since they will the subject of grace to be the very substance of the soul, in which immediately it has its seat: but of charity, and of the other virtues the subject to be the powers of the soul, the mind, namely, and the will. For they think that grace so stands to the infused virtues, as the soul stands to its powers. And as the soul gives natural being to the body; but from it flow the powers, which are the instruments of the soul: so also grace, of which now is the question, gives to the soul a certain supernatural being: but from it in a certain manner flow the habits of the infused virtues, which are the proximate principles of supernatural operation.
pass_b: Thesis XXII. Thomas, the prince of the Roman School, and very many others teach that this justifying grace that makes pleasing is a quality really distinct from charity and from all the other habits of the virtues.

They hold that the subject of grace is the very substance of the soul, where it has its seat directly, while the subject of charity and the other virtues is the soul's powers, that is, the mind and the will. In their view grace stands to the infused virtues as the soul stands to its powers.

The soul gives natural being to the body, and from it flow the powers that are its instruments. In the same way the grace in question gives the soul a kind of supernatural being, and from it flow, in a manner, the habits of the infused virtues, which are the proximate principles of supernatural action.

lemmas.latin: qualitatem quandam realiter distinctam a charitate
lemmas.gloss: a certain quality really distinct from charity

lemmas.latin: gratiae subjectum esse ipsam animae substantiam
lemmas.gloss: the subject of grace to be the very substance of the soul

lemmas.latin: dare animae esse quoddam supernaturale
lemmas.gloss: gives to the soul a certain supernatural being

lemmas.latin: quae sunt principia proxima operationis supernaturalis
lemmas.gloss: which are the proximate principles of supernatural operation

choices.why: Scholastic: distinct as one thing from another, not merely in concept (ratione); contrasted with Durandus and Bellarmine in XXIII-XXIV.

notes: Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II, q. 110, aa. 3-4.

sections.title: Durandus: grace and charity differ only in name
sections.pass_a: XXIII. Some on the contrary, as Durandus, will that there is no difference at all between grace, and charity: and affirm that they are distinguished not even by reason, but by name alone. Nor that charity and grace are more distinct, than to be dear and to be pleasing. For it is called grace, because through it man becomes pleasing to God: but charity, because through it man is rendered dear to God.
pass_b: Thesis XXIII. Some, on the other hand, such as Durandus, hold that there is no difference at all between grace and charity. They say the two are not distinguished even in concept, only in name.

Charity and grace, on this view, are no more distinct than being dear and being pleasing: it is called grace because by it a man becomes pleasing (gratus) to God, and charity because by it he is made dear (charus) to God.

lemmas.latin: nihil omnino interesse volunt inter gratiam, & charitatem
lemmas.gloss: will that there is no difference at all between grace, and charity

lemmas.latin: ac nequidem ratione, sed solo nomine distingui affirmant
lemmas.gloss: and affirm that they are distinguished not even by reason, but by name alone

lemmas.latin: quam esse charum & gratum
lemmas.gloss: than to be dear and to be pleasing

choices.why: The scale of distinctions: real, of reason (conceptual), and merely verbal; Durandus allows only the last.

notes: Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 26.

sections.title: Bellarmine's middle way: one habit, distinct only in reason
sections.pass_a: XXIV. But others in great number stand on a middle way in a manner. For they say that grace and charity are neither altogether undistinguished, nor yet distinguished in reality, but only by reason. Namely this is their opinion, that one and the same habit, in the part in which it regards the subject, and adorns the man himself in whom it is, and renders him pleasing and lovable to God, is named grace: but in the part in which it regards the work, and makes the will prompt for loving God above all things, it is properly called charity. Which opinion is Bellarmine's book 1 of Grace and Free Choice chap. 6.
pass_b: Thesis XXIV. A great many others take a kind of middle way. They say that grace and charity are not wholly indistinct, yet are distinguished not in reality but only in concept.

Their view is that one and the same habit is called grace insofar as it looks to its subject, adorns the man in whom it dwells and makes him pleasing and lovable to God. Insofar as it looks to the work and makes the will ready to love God above all things, it is properly called charity. This is Bellarmine's view (De gratia et libero arbitrio, book 1, chapter 6).

lemmas.latin: mediam quodammodo viam insistunt
lemmas.gloss: stand on a middle way in a manner

lemmas.latin: neque tamen reipsa, sed solum ratione distingui
lemmas.gloss: nor yet distinguished in reality, but only by reason

lemmas.latin: qua parte vero respicit opus
lemmas.gloss: but in the part in which it regards the work

lemmas.latin: ad Deum super omnia diligendum

sections.title: Actual grace: internal, not external, helps
sections.pass_a: XXV. As regards actual grace, or, as Bellarmine speaks, the grace of special Help, that it may be understood what they designate by that name, it is to be noted first that the helps by which God helps man in acting, are wont in the Schools to be distinguished into internal, and external. External are occasions and opportunities of acting, examples, counsels, precepts, exhortations, and more which it would be long to pursue one by one: internal consist in certain motions of the mind. External helps do not pertain to that grace of which now is the question, but it is restricted to internal.
pass_b: Thesis XXV. As for actual grace, or the grace of special help as Bellarmine calls it, to see what they mean by the term we must first note that the schools usually divide the helps by which God assists a man in acting into internal and external.

External helps are occasions and opportunities for acting, examples, counsels, precepts, exhortations and many others it would take too long to go through one by one. Internal helps consist in certain motions of the soul. External helps have nothing to do with the grace now in question, which is confined to the internal ones.

lemmas.gloss: the helps by which God helps man in acting

lemmas.gloss: more which it would be long to pursue one by one

lemmas.latin: interna in quibusdam animi motibus consistunt
lemmas.gloss: internal consist in certain motions of the mind

lemmas.latin: sed ad interna restringitur
lemmas.gloss: but it is restricted to internal

choices.why: Bellarmine's name for actual grace: God's passing motion helping a man to acts beyond his nature's power.

sections.title: General and special help; Bellarmine's definition
sections.pass_a: XXVI. Again that internal help of God, which men need in acting, the Roman School distinguishes into General and into special. They call general help, that by which God concurs with all creatures, and cooperates with them in acting, whether they act well, or even badly: whether the things which they do are within the powers and measure of nature, or surpass nature to some extent. For according to the common sense of the Roman School, in bad acts themselves what is positive is good, nor can it come to be except with God cooperating. But special help is called, that which is not given by God, except for good acts, and which exceed the powers of nature. And accordingly the grace of special help is defined by Bellarmine, The Motion of God by which man is helped to operations, which surpass his nature in some way.
pass_b: Thesis XXVI. The Roman School further divides this internal help of God, which men need in order to act, into general and special. General help is the help by which God concurs with all creatures and works with them in their acting, whether they act well or badly, and whether what they do lies within the powers and scope of nature or goes somewhat beyond it.

For in the common view of the Roman School whatever is positive even in evil acts is good, and cannot come about without God's cooperation. Special help is help that God gives only for good acts that exceed the powers of nature.
So Bellarmine defines the grace of special help as 'the motion of God by which man is helped toward actions that in some way surpass his nature'.

lemmas.latin: sive bene, sive etiam male agant
lemmas.gloss: whether they act well, or even badly

lemmas.latin: in ipsis malis actibus quod positivum est bonum est
lemmas.gloss: in bad acts themselves what is positive is good

lemmas.latin: quod non datur a Deo, nisi ad actus bonos
lemmas.gloss: which is not given by God, except for good acts

lemmas.latin: Motio Dei qua homo ad operationes, quae naturam suam aliquo modo superant, adjuvatur
lemmas.gloss: The Motion of God by which man is helped to operations, which surpass his nature in some way

choices.why: General help is God's concurrence with every creature's act, good or bad; special help is given only for good acts that exceed nature.

notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia et libero arbitrio (Controversiae, De gratia primi hominis ... et de libero arbitrio), book 1.

sections.title: Three ways an act surpasses nature's powers (Bellarmine)
sections.pass_a: XXVII. But he observes that some operation can surpass the powers of nature in three ways. First simply and absolutely. As if the operation from its own kind is of a higher order than natural things are. Such are the acts of the Theological virtues of faith, hope, and charity, which are not acquired through repeated and frequented acts, but are divinely infused into the soul. Second not simply, but by reason of the state of sin; because man weakened through sin cannot easily effect many things without such help. Third by reason of mode, place, time, or of any other circumstance whatever: because it can happen, that that which neither from its kind, nor by reason of state, surpasses the powers of nature, yet surpasses them by reason of circumstance. So, he says, a just man will be able easily to fulfil some precept of the Decalogue, if no diabolical temptation comes from without. But if temptation of this kind comes, without special help he will not be able to do it.
pass_b: Thesis XXVII. Bellarmine observes that an action can surpass the powers of nature in three ways. The first is simply and absolutely, when the action is by its kind of a higher order than natural things. Such are the acts of the theological virtues of faith, hope and charity, which are not acquired by repeated practice but are infused into the soul by God.
The second is not simply but because of the state of sin, since man, weakened by sin, cannot easily do many things without such help.

The third is because of manner, place, time or some other circumstance: something that does not exceed nature's powers by its kind or because of man's state may still exceed them because of the circumstances. 'So,' he says, 'a righteous man will easily be able to keep some commandment of the Decalogue if no temptation from the devil comes upon him from outside. But if such temptation comes, he will not be able to do it without special help.'

lemmas.latin: tribus modis naturae vires superare posse
lemmas.gloss: can surpass the powers of nature in three ways

lemmas.latin: quae non acquiruntur per iteratos & frequentatos actus
lemmas.gloss: which are not acquired through repeated and frequented acts

lemmas.latin: homo per peccatum debilitatus multa non potest sine tali auxilio facile efficere

sections.title: Actual grace: the good motions God stirs in us
sections.pass_a: XXVIII. And so to actual grace pertain, from the opinion of the doctors of the Roman School, all the good and salutary motions, which God excites in our minds. Which motions are both God's, because they proceed from him: and ours also, because they are vital actions, elicited from our faculties, God moving in a special manner.
pass_b: Thesis XXVIII. In the view of the doctors of the Roman School, then, actual grace covers all the good and saving motions God stirs up in our souls.
These motions are God's, because they come from him. They are ours too, because they are vital acts drawn out of our own faculties as God moves them in a special way.

lemmas.latin: omnes boni & salutares motus, quos in animis nostris Deus excitat
lemmas.gloss: all the good and salutary motions, which God excites in our minds

lemmas.latin: quoniam sunt actiones vitales
lemmas.gloss: because they are vital actions

lemmas.latin: Deo speciali modo movente, elicitae
lemmas.gloss: elicited, God moving in a special manner

choices.why: Acts that come from within a living agent's own powers; so the motions are truly ours even though God moves them.

sections.title: Motions of intellect and of will
sections.pass_a: XXIX. But those good motions, either regard the intellect, such as are internal illuminations and pious thoughts sent in by God, and in one word any illustrations and inspirations, by which the mind is led into the knowledge of saving truth: or the will, as pious desires and salutary motions and affections, by which the will is immediately affected.
pass_b: Thesis XXIX. These good motions concern either the intellect or the will. Those of the intellect are inward illuminations and devout thoughts sent by God, in a word any enlightenings and inspirations that lead the mind to know saving truth.
Those of the will are devout desires and saving motions and affections that touch the will directly.

lemmas.latin: vel intellectum spectant
lemmas.gloss: either regard the intellect

lemmas.latin: quibus mens in veritatis salutiferae notitiam ducitur
lemmas.gloss: by which the mind is led into the knowledge of saving truth

lemmas.latin: quibus immediate voluntas afficitur
lemmas.gloss: by which the will is immediately affected

choices.why: Illustrationes are acts of light on the intellect; inspirationes, motions on the will and mind; both are God's direct action.

sections.title: Gregory of Valencia: God's motions and our responses
sections.pass_a: XXX. But again Gregory of Valencia, for the sake of clearer doctrine, distinguishes the motions which are reduced to actual grace, into two kinds. One, he says, is contained in those motions, by which God excites, calls, and invites our minds, that they may be converted to him through faith, hope, charity, repentance, and actions of this sort. The other is contained in these motions, or actions, by which we respond to God exciting, calling, and inviting, and open the door of our mind, when we are converted to him. Tome 2 Disput. 8 question 3 point 2.
pass_b: Thesis XXX. Gregory of Valencia, to make the teaching clearer, divides the motions that belong to actual grace into two kinds.

'One kind,' he says, 'consists of the motions by which God rouses, calls and invites our minds to turn to him through faith, hope, charity, repentance and acts of that sort. The other consists of the motions or acts by which we answer God as he rouses, calls and invites us, and open the door of our mind when we turn to him' (tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 2).

lemmas.latin: clarioris doctrinae causa
lemmas.gloss: for the sake of clearer doctrine

lemmas.latin: quibus Deus mentes nostras excitat, vocat, & invitat
lemmas.gloss: by which God excites, calls, and invites our minds

lemmas.latin: aperimus mentis nostrae januam
lemmas.gloss: open the door of our mind

sections.title: Indeliberate and deliberate motions
sections.pass_a: XXXI. Motions of the former kind, according to him, are indeliberate, and only physically not freely elicited from our faculties: but of the latter are free and deliberate. To the former kind pertain pious thoughts and pious desires, sent in immediately by God without our consent: but to the latter, all the acts of Christian virtues, which by the help of God's grace we elicit.
pass_b: Thesis XXXI. According to him, the motions of the first kind are indeliberate: our faculties produce them only physically, not freely. Those of the second kind are free and deliberate.

The first kind covers devout thoughts and devout desires that God sends directly, without our consent. The second covers all the acts of the Christian virtues that we bring forth with the help of God's grace.

lemmas.latin: sunt indeliberati, & physice tantum non libere a facultatibus nostris eliciti
lemmas.gloss: are indeliberate, and only physically not freely elicited from our faculties

lemmas.latin: absque nostro consensu immediate a Deo immissa
lemmas.gloss: sent in immediately by God without our consent

lemmas.latin: quos Dei gratia juvante elicimus
lemmas.gloss: which by the help of God's grace we elicit

sections.title: Rousing and assisting grace: Bellarmine and the Jesuits
sections.pass_a: XXXII. Besides the grace of special help, or, as it is called by others, actual, is wont to be divided into exciting grace, and helping grace; or, as Bellarmine speaks, into exciting help, and helping help. Which distinction is not expounded in the same manner by the Theologians of the Roman School. Bellarmine, and all the Jesuits with him, and very many others, say that to exciting grace, which they also call calling, pertain divine illustrations, and inspirations, by which God knocks at our heart, that we may be roused from the sleep of sin, or of negligence in good works. But to helping grace, or of helping help, they say belongs divine cooperation, direction, and protection, by which we are helped, both that we choose, and that we do what God going before inspired. According to that Apoc. 3. Behold I stand at the door and knock, if anyone hears my voice, I will come in to him, etc. Which are the words of Bellarmine book 1 of free Choice chap. 2.
pass_b: Thesis XXXII. The grace of special help, or actual grace as others call it, is usually divided into rousing grace and assisting grace, or in Bellarmine's terms into rousing help and assisting help. The theologians of the Roman School do not all explain this distinction the same way.

Bellarmine and all the Jesuits with him, and very many others, say that rousing grace, which they also call calling grace, covers the divine enlightenings and inspirations by which God knocks at our heart to wake us from the sleep of sin or of slackness in good works.

Assisting grace, or the grace of assisting help, they say, covers God's cooperation, guidance and protection, by which we are helped both to choose and to do what God, going before us, has inspired. So Revelation 3: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice, I will come in to him', and so on. These are Bellarmine's words (book 1, On Free Choice, chapter 2).

lemmas.latin: non eodem modo a Theologis Scholae Romanae exponitur
lemmas.gloss: is not expounded in the same manner by the Theologians of the Roman School

sections.title: Gregory of Valencia agrees: calling and assisting grace
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. And to the same comes back the exposition of Gregory of Valencia. For calling grace, or exciting, he says, Theologians call certain divine inspirations, or certain motions divinely excited in the mind of man, by which God allures and invites man to himself, and moves him to pious and salutary actions, that by acts of faith, hope, charity, and repentance he may be converted. But helping grace they call, the gifts and benefits of God, by which God helps man consenting to the divine calling and exciting, both in that very thing that he consents and is converted, and in other actions of piety, through which one strives toward blessedness. And so to this helping grace pertains in the first place that God by a peculiar concurrence cooperates with man to conversion, that is, to believing, hoping, loving, repenting, etc. Likewise that he guards man with singular care and providence, and protects him from evil, and directs and stimulates him to good, and to him by various inspirations, gives strength for conquering temptations, and for observing the commandments. Tom. 2 disput. 8 quaest. 3 punct. 3.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIII. Gregory of Valencia's account comes to the same thing. 'Theologians,' he says, 'give the name calling or rousing grace to certain divine inspirations, motions stirred up by God in a man's mind, by which God draws and invites the man to himself and moves him to devout and saving actions, so that he may turn to God by acts of faith, hope, charity and repentance.

They call assisting grace those gifts and benefits by which God helps a man who consents to the divine calling and rousing: both in the very act of consenting and turning, and in the other acts of devotion by which one presses on toward blessedness.

So this assisting grace includes first of all God's special concurrence with man in conversion, that is, in believing, hoping, loving, repenting and so on. It also includes his guarding man with particular care and providence, protecting him from evil, directing and spurring him to good, and giving him strength through various inspirations to overcome temptations and keep the commandments' (tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 3).
